652.title: Partners, all
652.hook: all are partners in Your grace; You are outside no one (Majh M5, ang 97)
652.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Majh shabad of the common Master in kirtan; the line about all being partners is often cited for langar and for gurdwaras open to everyone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, darshan, and your line: the whole longing. Did you finish your letter? Today, one page further on in Guru Arjan's Majh hymns, a single word that turns strangers into partners. Day six hundred fifty-two.

Punjabi villages remember the sanjha chulha, a shared clay oven in the open. Women from different households brought their dough, sat together, slapped rotis onto the hot walls, and talked while the bread puffed. Nobody owned the fire. Everybody used it. Sanjha means shared, held in common. And Guru Arjan, in a hymn on the same page where his letters home end, takes that everyday village word and uses it to describe the whole human race.
screen: `A SHARED CLAY OVEN.` → `NOBODY OWNED THE FIRE.` → `SANJHA: HELD IN COMMON.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Majh, on ang 97. It opens, in effect: You are our common Master, our Father. Your storehouse holds the nine treasures, and it never runs out. Whoever You give to is satisfied. Then come the lines the outline points to: all place their hope in You; You dwell in every heart. All are called partners, saanjheevaal, in Your grace. You are seen outside no one. Saanjheevaal is built from that same word, saanjh: a share, a partnership. It's the word for people who hold something together, like farmers who share a well or a team of oxen. Guru Arjan says every person is a shareholder in the same grace. Not guests. Not customers. Partners. Think about what a partner is. A partner isn't someone you tolerate or help out of pity. A partner has an equal claim. The well is as much theirs as yours. And then the second half: You are seen outside no one. In the hymn, there is no person in whom the One is absent. Put the two lines together and you have the ground under a lot of Sikh practice. Sikhs often point to lines like these to explain why langar feeds anyone, why the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is known for doors on all four sides, open to all comers, and why the Ardas ends with good for all. Not because everyone is the same. People are wildly different. But because nobody is outside the partnership. In the hymn's terms, the stranger in the next seat on the bus holds the same share in grace.
screen: `OUR COMMON MASTER AND FATHER.` · `SAANJHEEVAAL: PARTNERS, SHAREHOLDERS.` · `YOU ARE OUTSIDE NO ONE.` · `NOBODY OUTSIDE THE PARTNERSHIP.` · then, large: `ALL PARTNERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Bring to mind a stranger you'll probably see today: a bus driver, a cashier, a coworker you've never really talked to, someone in your building. Picture their face. Now hold Guru Arjan's word over them: partner. Not a background extra in your day. In the hymn's word, a shareholder in the same grace. Notice if anything shifts in how you'd greet them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with their face in mind. The bell holds the time.
Partners. Saanjheevaal: in Guru Arjan's hymn, everyone holds an equal share in the One's grace, and the One is outside no one.
Your line: all partners. Today, treat one stranger as a partner: learn their name, ask their opinion, or share something you'd usually keep. Day six hundred fifty-two.

653.title: You are my father
653.hook: You are my father, You are my mother, You my kin and my brother (Majh M5, ang 103)
653.howItsDone: Guru Arjan's 'toon meraa pitaa toonhai meraa maataa' is sung in kirtan, taught to children, and turned to in times of trouble.

segments.voice: Yesterday, partners, and your line: all partners. Which stranger did you treat as one? Today, a few pages on in Guru Arjan's Majh hymns, partners become family. Day six hundred fifty-three.

Father. Mother. Kin. Brother. Four plain family words, one after another, and that is how this hymn of Guru Arjan opens. A child could sing that list after one hearing. An adult sitting in a hospital corridor at three in the morning could say it too, and mean something a child can't yet know. The words stay the same; the person singing them keeps changing. Today, a hymn with room for every age of a life.
screen: `FOUR PLAIN FAMILY WORDS.` → `A CHILD COULD SING IT.` → `SO COULD A HOSPITAL CORRIDOR.`

segments.voice: The shabad is Guru Arjan's, in Raag Majh, on ang 103. It begins, in effect: You are my father, You are my mother. You are my kin, You are my brother. You are my protector in every place, so what fear, what worry, can touch me? The second stanza: by Your grace I come to know You. You are my shelter, You are my honor. Without You there is no other; all of this is Your play, Your arena. Listen to two words in that second stanza: ot, shelter, and maan, honor. We met them in the Ardas, three weeks ago: the honor of the dishonored, the shelter of the shelterless. Same words. Here Guru Arjan says them in the first person. You are my shelter. You are my honor. Now, why family words? Guru Arjan had a father and mother. He had brothers, and one of them, Prithi Chand, tradition says, kept back his letters home. Families hold the deepest love and sometimes the deepest hurt. The shabad doesn't pretend otherwise. What it does is name the One as every kind of family at once: the father who provides, the mother who holds, the kin who belong to you, the brother who stands next to you. Whatever a person has or lacks in their own family, the hymn offers the same thing: you are not without family. And from there it reasons straight to fearlessness. If the One is all of these, everywhere, then fear has nowhere to stand. That's not a promise that nothing hard will happen. In the hymn, it's a promise about who is there when it does.
screen: `FATHER, MOTHER, KIN, BROTHER.` · `MY PROTECTOR IN EVERY PLACE.` · `OT AND MAAN, AS IN THE ARDAS.` · `SO WHAT FEAR CAN TOUCH ME?` · then, large: `YOU ARE MY FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit and let the family words come one at a time: father, mother, kin, brother. With each, notice what rises: warmth, ache, absence, gratitude. Let it be whatever it is. Then, if you pray, you can say the line to the One, slowly, in English or Punjabi: You are my father, You are my mother. If you don't pray, simply rest with the thought that you are not without family, and let one person who has been family to you come to mind. The bell holds the time.
Pitaa, father: Guru Arjan names the One as pitaa, mother, kin and brother, protector everywhere, and asks, so what fear can touch me?
Your line: you are my family. Today, when you feel alone or afraid, say it once under your breath. And call one person who has been family to you. Day six hundred fifty-three.

654.title: Make mercy your mosque
654.hook: make mercy your mosque, faith your prayer mat, honest earning your Qur'an (Majh ki Var M1, ang 140)
654.howItsDone: Sikhs sing and recite Majh ki Var in the gurdwara, and often cite this salok of Guru Nanak as teaching that every outward practice is fulfilled through mercy, faith and honest living.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pitaa, and your line: you are my family. Who did you call? Today Guru Nanak speaks to a Muslim friend in the words of his friend's own faith. Day six hundred fifty-four.

Guru Nanak spent his life among both Muslims and Hindus. Tradition remembers his companion on the road, Bhai Mardana, as a Muslim musician who played the rabab beside him. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak often speaks to people in the language of their own practice. To Hindus he talks about the sacred thread, the pilgrimage, the lamp. To Muslims he talks about the mosque, the prayer mat, the fast. And in one salok in Majh ki Var, he builds a whole mosque without using a single brick.
screen: `AMONG MUSLIMS AND HINDUS.` → `IN THE LANGUAGE OF THEIR PRACTICE.` → `A MOSQUE WITHOUT A BRICK.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 140. It goes, in effect: make mercy your mosque, faith your prayer mat, and what is honest and rightfully earned your Qur'an. Make modesty and good conduct your observances and your fast; so become a Muslim. Make good deeds your Kaaba, truth your guide, and good works your creed and your prayer. Let your rosary be whatever pleases Him. Then, Nanak, He will keep your honor. The word for mercy is mihar: kindness, compassion. Now, what is this doing? It would be easy to hear it wrongly, as Guru Nanak telling Muslims to give up their mosques. That's not what the text says. Guru Nanak doesn't ask anyone to stop praying, fasting or going to the mosque. He's asking what all of it is for, and answering: mercy, faith, honest living, truth, good deeds. It's the same move he makes toward Hindus in Asa di Var, where he describes a sacred thread spun from compassion and contentment. In both, he speaks from inside the listener's own words. For Sikhs, the same question turns right back on themselves. What makes a gurdwara a gurdwara? What is the turban for, the Ardas, the langar? Read that way, the salok's question fits every house of worship, a gurdwara included. A person can kneel on the finest prayer mat in the world, or bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, and still need to ask whether mercy came in with them.
screen: `MIHAR: MERCY, COMPASSION.` · `MERCY THE MOSQUE, FAITH THE MAT.` · `NOT GIVING IT UP: FILLING IT.` · `THE QUESTION TURNS BACK ON SIKHS.` · then, large: `MERCY IS THE MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of the place where you pray, or rest, or go to find quiet: a mosque, a gurdwara, a church, a bench by a lake, your own bedroom. Picture walking in. Now ask Guru Nanak's question: did mercy come in with me? Then think of one merciful act you could do today, small and real: a patient answer, a meal shared, a debt forgiven, a kind word to someone struggling. If you pray, you can say Waheguru and hold that act before the One. The bell holds the time.
Mihar, mercy, kindness: Guru Nanak, speaking in Islam's own words, makes it the mosque, faith the prayer mat, honest living the Qur'an.
Your line: mercy is the mosque. Today, do one merciful act before you enter any place you call holy, or before you sleep. Day six hundred fifty-four.

screen: `DAY 654 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOU SPENT THE NIGHT SLEEPING.`

655.title: You spent the night sleeping
655.hook: the night lost in sleep, the day in eating; a jewel of a life traded for a shell (Gauri M1, ang 156)
655.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Gauri shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its opening lines about a diamond life traded for a cowrie are often quoted as a call to remember the Name each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mihar, and your line: mercy is the mosque. What merciful act did you carry in? Today, two lines from Guru Nanak about the price of a day. Day six hundred fifty-five.

Sunday night, ten o'clock. The weekend you'd been looking forward to since Wednesday is over. You slept late on Saturday. There was a long lunch, then a nap, then dinner, and somehow it was Sunday afternoon. Try to name one thing from it you'd want to remember, and it takes a while. Nothing went wrong. It just went. Guru Nanak looked at days like that five hundred years ago, and he priced them in the cheapest currency he knew.
screen: `SUNDAY NIGHT, TEN O'CLOCK.` → `NOTHING WENT WRONG. IT JUST WENT.` → `PRICED IN THE CHEAPEST CURRENCY.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Gauri, on ang 156. It begins, in effect: the night you wasted sleeping, the day you wasted eating. This life, precious as a diamond, is being traded away for a shell. The word is kaudi, a cowrie shell. In Guru Nanak's world, cowries were the smallest small change, the coin you'd barely bother to pick up. So picture a merchant walking into the market with a diamond and walking out with a cowrie, and calling it a day. Then the refrain: you didn't come to know the Name of the Lord, and afterward, foolish one, you'll regret it. Now, a fair note. Guru Nanak isn't against sleep, or food. The Gurus lived as householders and ate with everyone in the langar. Elsewhere Gurbani speaks well of sleeping little and eating little, but the point here is sharper. Sleeping and eating aren't the waste. The waste is when that's all a day becomes: one need met after another, and the diamond never spent on what it was for. In Sikh teaching, what it's for is naam, remembering the One, alongside honest work and sharing. And notice the tone. It's not quite a scolding. It's the alarm of a friend watching you about to make a terrible trade. Kaudi, a shell, for heera, a diamond. The trade isn't final yet. Today is still in your hand, and the shabad is asking you to look at it before you spend it.
screen: `THE NIGHT IN SLEEP, THE DAY IN EATING.` · `KAUDI: THE SMALLEST COIN.` · `A DIAMOND TRADED FOR A SHELL.` · `THE TRADE ISN'T FINAL YET.` · then, large: `NOT FOR A SHELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one hour. Look ahead at the rest of today. Find one hour, just one, that usually drifts away: on the phone, in front of the television, half-working, half-scrolling. Now decide, here, what that hour will be traded for instead. A walk with someone. A real conversation. A page of reading. Some quiet remembering, Waheguru on the breath. Picture yourself spending it that way. Notice how a single hour, chosen, feels heavier than three that just happen. The bell holds the time.
Kaudi, a cowrie shell, the smallest coin: Guru Nanak's warning, the night in sleep, the day in eating, and a diamond of a life traded for one.
Your line: not for a shell. Today, spend the hour you chose the way you chose it. When you catch yourself drifting, say the line. Day six hundred fifty-five.

656.title: A child is born
656.hook: Guru Arjan's joy at the birth of his son Hargobind (Asa M5, ang 396)
656.howItsDone: Sikh families sing Guru Arjan's 'satgur saachai deeaa bhej' at the birth of a child, and bring the newborn to the gurdwara for an Ardas of thanks and the naming ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaudi, and your line: not for a shell. How did you spend the hour you chose? Today, the happiest kind of hour there is. Day six hundred fifty-six.

The text arrives at 4:12 in the morning: a photo of a tiny, furious, red-faced person in a striped hospital blanket. Name to follow. Everyone's fine. And suddenly the whole family group chat is awake, typing in capital letters. Some joy can't wait for a polite hour. Tradition says Guru Arjan knew that kind of joy in a village near Amritsar, when his wife, Mata Ganga, gave birth to a son after long waiting. And his answer to that joy was a song.
screen: `A PHOTO AT 4:12 A.M.` → `THE GROUP CHAT WAKES UP.` → `GURU ARJAN SINGS.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Asa, on ang 396. It begins, in effect: the True Guru has sent this child. The long-lived one has been born, by destiny. He came to dwell in the womb, and his mother's heart is full of delight. Then the refrain: a son is born, a devotee of the Lord; what was written from the beginning is now revealed to all. And then: in the tenth month, by the Lord's command, the child was born. Sorrow is gone, great joy has come, and the companions sing the Guru's hymns in delight. The child was Hargobind, who would become the sixth Guru. Some hear a gentle play in the refrain: bhagat govind, a devotee of Govind, the Lord, and the boy named Hargobind. Notice where the credit goes. The child is a gift, sent. The joy is real and physical, a mother's delight, a household singing. But the first line points past the parents to the Giver. Sikh families sing this shabad at births, and bring a newborn to the gurdwara for an Ardas of thanks. And because the hymn says son, a fair note: Gurbani gives a daughter no lesser place. Guru Nanak asked, in Asa di Var, why anyone would speak ill of woman, from whom kings are born. Families sing this same shabad for a girl too. A child is a gift arriving, whoever the child is.
screen: `THE TRUE GURU HAS SENT THIS CHILD.` · `A MOTHER'S HEART FULL OF DELIGHT.` · `HARGOBIND, THE SIXTH GURU.` · `DAUGHTERS WELCOMED WITH THE SAME JOY.` · then, large: `A GIFT ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Bring to mind a new parent you know, or a child recently born in your circle, or even someone expecting. If no one comes, remember a baby you once held. Picture the child's face, the parents' tired, astonished eyes. Let yourself feel glad for them, without any if or but. If you pray, you can thank the One for the gift, or ask a long life for the child with a quiet Waheguru. Then think of how you'll tell them you're glad. The bell holds the time.
A child is born. Guru Arjan's song at the birth of Hargobind: the True Guru has sent this child; sorrow is gone, great joy has come.
Your line: a gift arrives. Today, congratulate a new parent with a real message, not just a heart emoji. Tell them one thing you hope for their child. Day six hundred fifty-six.

screen: `DAY 656 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ONE FATHER, ALL HIS CHILDREN.`

657.title: One father, all his children
657.hook: ek pitaa ekas ke ham baarik: one Father, and we are all His children (Sorath M5, ang 611)
657.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Sorath shabad with 'ek pitaa ekas ke ham baarik' in kirtan, and the line is quoted for the kinship of all people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a child is born, and your line: a gift arrives. Who did you congratulate? Today Guru Arjan widens the family from one child to every child. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

Siblings are complicated. They borrow your clothes without asking. They know exactly which button to push. They tell your secrets at Thanksgiving. And yet, let anyone outside the family say a word against them, and something fierce can wake up. Siblings don't choose each other. They're handed to each other by having the same parents. Guru Arjan took that simple fact and stretched it, in one line of Raag Sorath, across every human being alive.
screen: `SIBLINGS ARE COMPLICATED.` → `YOU DON'T CHOOSE EACH OTHER.` → `STRETCHED ACROSS EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: The line is on ang 611: ek pitaa ekas ke ham baarik, tu meraa gur haaee. One Father; we are children of the One. You are my Guru. Ek is one. Pitaa, father, the same word we met in You are my father. Baarik, children, little ones. And it goes on, in effect: listen, my friend, my soul is a sacrifice to you; show me a glimpse of the Lord. Four days ago Guru Arjan called the One father, mother, kin and brother. That was vertical: me and the One. This line turns sideways. If there is one Father, then everyone else is a brother or a sister. You don't get to choose them, any more than you chose the ones at your own family table. Notice he doesn't say we're all alike, or that we all agree, or that we'll all get along. Real siblings don't. The hymn makes a smaller and harder claim: we belong to each other, because we belong to the same One. And nobody applies to be a sibling. Nobody earns a seat at the family table, and nobody can be voted off it. If there is one Father, the line has no membership test: the person you like least is as much a child of the One as the person you admire most. Then the next line turns to friendship. Guru Arjan speaks to a friend, meetaa, and asks for help to see the One. In the hymn, the others aren't only people to be kind to. They can be the ones who help a person find the Father.
screen: `EK PITAA: ONE FATHER.` · `BAARIK: WE ARE ALL CHILDREN.` · `NOT ALIKE, BUT BELONGING.` · `A FRIEND WHO HELPS ME SEE THE ONE.` · then, large: `ALL HIS CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Bring to mind someone very different from you: different politics, different faith, different age, someone you find a little hard. See their face. Now hold Guru Arjan's line over the two of you: one Father, and we are children of the One. Don't force a warm feeling. Just try on the word sibling. Notice what resists, and what softens. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for both of you at once. The bell holds the time.
One father. Ek pitaa ekas ke ham baarik: one Father, and we are all children of the One, and in the hymn, every stranger is a sibling.
Your line: all his children. Today, when a stranger annoys you, say the line once in your head, and treat them the way you'd treat a sibling in public. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

658.title: Whatever you ask
658.hook: whatever you ask of your own Master, He gives (Dhanasri M5, ang 681)
658.tomorrow: As the Word comes to me, Lalo
658.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Dhanasri shabad in kirtan and often recall its line 'jo maageh thaakur apune te soee soee devai' when making an Ardas, alongside acceptance of the Will.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one father, and your line: all his children. Which stranger did you treat like a sibling? Today, the week closes with a bold promise about asking. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

A kid with a request runs the numbers fast: one parent for the late curfew, the other for the money, a grandparent for the extra dessert. Asking is a skill. You learn who will say yes, and how to phrase it, and when to wait. Then one day, in Raag Dhanasri, you come across a line from Guru Arjan that seems to skip all of that strategy: whatever you ask of your own Master, He gives. No angles. No timing. It sounds almost too simple. So what is it actually saying?
screen: `WHICH PARENT TO ASK.` → `ASKING IS A SKILL.` → `WHATEVER YOU ASK, HE GIVES.`

segments.voice: The line is on ang 681: jo maageh thaakur apune te, soee soee devai. Whatever is asked of one's own Master, that very thing He gives. And it continues, in effect: whatever the servant Nanak speaks, it comes true, here and hereafter. Thaakur is master, lord, the one you belong to. Notice the small word apune, your own. Not a distant ruler you petition through officials. Your own Master, the one who already knows you. Now, the honest question. Does this mean a person gets anything they want? The hymn itself gives the context. The one speaking is the daas, the servant: Nanak calls himself that in the very next line. One reading is that a servant who lives close to the Master starts to want what the Master wants. Elsewhere Gurbani speaks of bhaana, the Will, and of asking first for the Name. So the line is less a blank check than a picture of trust between a servant and a good master: the servant isn't afraid to ask, and the Master doesn't hold back. Some Sikhs also say, from experience, that what's given is sometimes not what was asked, but what was needed: strength instead of escape, patience instead of speed. Look back at the week. Partners, all: everyone holds a share. Pitaa. Mihar. Kaudi: not for a shell. A child is born, a gift arrives. One father, all his children. And now: thaakur. A week about belonging, and about asking like someone who belongs.
screen: `THAAKUR: YOUR OWN MASTER.` · `THE SERVANT WHO ASKS IN TRUST.` · `NOT A BLANK CHECK: THE WILL.` · `THIS WEEK: BELONGING, THEN ASKING.` · then, large: `ASK YOUR MASTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for one good thing. Sit quietly and let your wants come up, all of them, the big and the petty. Don't judge them. Then let them settle, and see which one is truly good: good for you and good for others. Maybe it's courage, or healing for someone, or patience with a child. Choose that one. If you pray, you can ask the One for it simply, the way a child asks a parent they trust. If you don't, hold it as a hope. The bell holds the time.
Thaakur, master, lord, the one you belong to: Guru Arjan says whatever is asked of your own thaakur, He gives; the trust of a servant who belongs.
Your line: ask your master. Today, ask plainly for one good thing, from the One if you pray, or from a person you trust. Then notice what's given. Day six hundred fifty-eight.
